BYD third-generation Tang EV (Source: China MIIT)
BYD’s new Tang EV, its “tech-savvy” flagship five-seat SUV, was revealed in a regulatory filing with dual electric motors delivering a combined 690 horsepower. The interior is even more impressive.
BYD prepares to launch the new Tang EV
The third-generation Tang will join the recent Da Tang (“Great Tang”) as BYD expands its flagship electric SUV lineup.
Ahead of its expected launch later this year, the new Tang was revealed in the latest batch of proposed vehicles for sale by China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT).
According to the filing, the third-generation Tang is 5,045 mm long, 1,980 mm wide, and 1,740 mm tall, with a 2,950 mm wheelbase, or 145 mm longer than its predecessor.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Unlike the current Tang, which offers five- and six-seat configurations, the new version will be a 5-seater only.
It uses a dual-motor, all-wheel-drive powertrain. The front electric motor produces 288 horsepower (215 kW), while the rear delivers 402 horsepower (300 kW) for a combined output of up to 690 horsepower (515 kW).
The filing reveals it will use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supplied by BYD’s Wuwei Fudi Battery Co.
Although it wasn’t in the release, the third-generation Tang EV will use BYD’s Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, enabling it to charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes.
It will be available in two battery packs: 88.682 kWh and 105.792 kWh, delivering CLTC ranges of 730 km (453 miles), 830 km (515 miles), and 850 km (528 miles), depending on the configuration.
After it debuted at the Chengdu Auto Show in August, Lu Tian, General Manager of BYD’s Dynasty lineup, revealed the first official interior images earlier this month.
The “8-series, five-seat, tech-savvy flagship SUV,” as Lu called it, features two massive screens. One is a stretched 35.4″ integrated display, and the other is a 30″ panoramic screen. It will be available in two interior color schemes: Dune Beige and Amber Brown.
BYD third-generation Tang electric SUV interior (Source: Lu Tian)
Like many flagship models nowadays, the new Tang features zero-gravity captain’s chairs in the second row. Lu said the five-seat SUV will provide over 1,000 mm of second-row legroom.
It’s also loaded with BYD’s premium tech and other features, including its DiSus-A intelligent body control system with a dual-chamber air suspension, and its God’s Eye B advanced driving assistance system.
BYD third-generation Tang electric SUV interior (Source: Lu Tian)
BYD is expected to launch the third-generation Tang by the end of 2026. Since the full-size Great Tang starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500), the five-seater will likely offer a smaller, more affordable alternative.
In its first three months on the market, BYD has sold over 10,000 units of the flagship full-size SUV.

Air Canada on Monday announced the expansion of its freighter network for the upcoming winter season, adding new service from its Toronto global hub to Amsterdam, Monterrey, Mexico, and Panama City, Panama.
The additions provide customers with dedicated , large-pallet capacity on key transatlantic and Latin American trade lanes, and create additional routing options between Europe, Canada and Latin America.
The twice-weekly service to Amsterdam begins Oct. 29, Air Canada Cargo ( TSX: AC ) said in a news release.
Service to Amsterdam complements Air Canada’s passenger flights to the city, while Monterrey and Panama City deepen freighter connectivity to important manufacturing and distribution markets in Mexico and Central America.
Air Canada operates six Boeing 767-300 freighter aircraft and manages cargo shipped on passenger aircraft. In the second quarter, ended June 30, cargo revenue increased 28.4% to $229.8 million. Cargo revenue was up 16% for the first half to $413 million.
Management said the increases were primarily driven by higher cargo yields and favorable freight pricing conditions, particularly on international routes, in part, due to higher carrier surcharges. Airlines like Air Canada have significantly increased fuel surcharges on cargo shipments to cope with the skyrocketing price of jet fuel in the wake of hostilities between the U.S., Israel and Iran in late February.
By comparison, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines, which don’t have freighter aircraft, recorded second-quarter cargo revenue of $294 million and $571 million, respectively. But the two American majors also have much larger global widebody networks than Air Canada.
Why It Matters: Freighter aircraft allow Air Canada to cover gaps in its widebody passenger network to cities that cargo shippers frequent.
“The introduction of our freighters in Amsterdam is an important step in strengthening our European network. This gives us dedicated main-deck capacity at a time of year when transatlantic capacity is more constrained, helping us better serve customers in the Netherlands and across Europe while creating opportunities to connect their cargo through our global network,” said Matthieu Casey, managing director, commercial – cargo, at Air Canada. Together with new freighter service to Monterrey and Panama City, these additions enhance two-way connectivity between Europe and our growing Latin American network, creating more opportunities to reach key markets such as Quito, Lima, Bogotá and Mexico City.”
Air Canada’s new freighter service to Monterrey begins Oct. 26, operating three times per week. Panama City service begins Oct. 25, with up to two flights per week, the company said.
In Mexico, the airline’s cargo jets also fly to Mexico City and Guadalajara.

Toyota Asks Europe To Change Which Vehicles Count as Zero-Emission and Locally Made
8 photos
Photo: Toyota
The world's largest automaker wants an internal combustion vehicle to qualify as zero-emission in Europe, provided it runs only on approved renewable fuels. That is the single most important request buried in the company's latest policy paper, ahead of all the requests that touch upon competitiveness and other topics. Toyota, in other words, is asking EU legislators to change how they count the vehicles manufacturers can sell in the European space.
The proposed VEEF category includes vehicles running exclusively on eligible fuels, not internal combustion vehicles whose owners choose a renewable blend once in a blue moon. Toyota wants one EU definition tied to the Renewable Energy Directive, namely RED III. Zero-emission would describe the vehicle's regulatory treatment under said proposal.
That request accompanies a push for a 90 percent reduction in new vehicle CO2 emissions by 2025 rather than 100 percent. Toyota wants renewable fuels and green steel to help close the remaining gap. However, it doesn't say that 10 percent of sales should automatically go to combustion vehicles. A fleet emissions reduction and a powertrain sales quota are different animals in the grand scheme of things.
Toyota is asking for more than a different endgame. Per the attached release, the automaker wants a five-year compliance window from 2028 to 2032 to smooth the transition through 2030 and 2031. A weak electric sales year could then sit alongside a stronger one instead of demanding that the factory plan, dealer allocations, and customer demand all fall into step at precisely the same moment.
As you might have already guessed, the company's case clearly rests on a forecast rather than a certainty. Toyota puts battery-electric vehicles at roughly 45 percent of new vehicle demand in 2030, whereas current rules mandate more than 55 percent. The gap is understandably wider for commercial vehicles.
Photo: Toyota The actual EU rule controls average CO2 emissions rather than a BEV quota. Toyota's argument is that the expected buying preferences and the emissions match don't line up. There is, however, a pretty evident commercial interest here. Toyota claims that manufacturers should focus their R&D budgets on technology rather than compliance, and I can fully understand where they're coming from.
More flexibility would also let automakers operating in the European bloc to manage their product mix with fewer dramatic adjustments when electric demand misses expectations. That's why Toyota asks for regular reviews if demand and infrastructure develop too slowly. It simply wants the timetable to follow the market far more closely than ever before.
Britain gets its own request, specifically maximum required zero-emission shares of 50 percent for cars and 40 percent for light commercial vehicles in 2030. Toyota wants those compliance options to continue through 2035, with flexibilities, mirroring the five-year approach for the EU. A completed mandate revision in 2027 is also mentioned.
Last but not least, Toyota's proposed 'Made with Europe' approach would recognize a limited group of customs-union and free-trade reciprocal partners. The press release attached below explicitly names Britain, Turkey, and Japan. The request concerns the Industrial Accelerator Act and eligibility across incentives, public procurement, and corporate fleet.
Toyota has invested in excess of 12 billion euros in Europe since 1990, and as of today, it directly employs more than 26,000 people. Toyota further proposes phasing European content up to 70 percent after three years, measured against ex-works vehicle value. Separately, it seeks a 70 percent overall vehicle sales threshold rather than the proposed 85 percent.

Mercedes-AMG GT 63 Is World's Most Powerful SUV, Steals the Show From Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric
20 photos
Photo: Mercedes-AMG | Porsche
Mercedes-AMG unveiled the GT SUV over the weekend and has made the ranking of the world’s most powerful SUVs shift. The range-topping GT 63 has just stolen the crown from Porsche’s top SUV, the Cayenne Turbo Electric, by a small margin: just 14 horsepower sets the two apart.
Here is the all-new Mercedes-AMG GT SUV , ready to give the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric a run for its money. It has now taken the lead as the world’s most powerful SUV, with its 1,153 horsepower (1,169 metric horsepower), 14 horsepower ahead of the Porsche SUV.
The Lucid Gravity GT-S rounds out the podium with its 1,070 horsepower (1,085 metric horsepower), while the Tesla Model X Plaid is trying to keep up with it with a factory rating of 1,020 horsepower (1,034 metric horsepower). The massive GMC Hummer EV comes in fifth with 1,000 horsepower (1,014 metric horsepower).
The battle of the numbers These are figures that automakers did not even dare to dream of before the electric revolution kicked off. Then, the battle of horsepower won over, as automakers started Nurburgring wars, duels of zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) or quarter-mile competitions.
Photo: Mercedes-AMG With its all-new GT 63 SUV, Mercedes-AMG had one single target: Porsche's pride and joy, the Cayenne Turbo Electric. It is the only one that, according to the numbers it can keep up with the first SUV entirely developed in Affalterbach and built in Sindelfingen. Both models bypass the traditional combustion engine power to deliver four-figure horsepower and hypercar-level acceleration.
The AMG GT 63 SUV is set in motion by a tri-motor setup with axial flux motors, two mounted out back within a single space-saving casing on the rear axle, and one on the front axle, acting like a booster unit. In the meantime, the Porsche comes with two electric motors, one up front and another out back. Both SUVs feature all-wheel drive.
Even though the Mercedes-AMG looks every inch a winner on paper, both models rocket from 0 to 60 mph in 2.4 seconds. The Mercedes maxes out at 168 mph (270 kph), while the digital speedometer of the Porsche stops at 162 mph (260 kph).
The powertrains are obviously heavy lifters, because the SUVs may be quick and agile, but they are not exactly ballerinas on the road. The Mercedes weighs 5,941 pounds (2,695 kilograms), while the Porsche is 110 pounds lighter, tipping the scales at 5,831 pounds (2,645 kilograms).
Photo: Porsche Both vehicles integrate high-voltage battery packs into the floor pan, positioned structurally between the front and rear axles. This "skateboard" layout lowers the center of gravity and balances weight across both axles, while ensuring the large packs do not intrude on cabin passenger or cargo space.
Bigger battery, more range for the Mercedes-AMG GT SUV Mercedes planted a massive 128-kWh battery pack, which stores enough energy for a drive of up to 435 miles (700 kilometers), before the GT 63 SUV needs to be plugged in again. That is the official WLTP rating. The EPA testing might slash up to 100 miles from that figure.
In the meantime, the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric is fitted with a slightly smaller 113 kW battery pack, which provides a WLTP range of up to 387 miles (623 kilometers) or roughly 330 miles (531 kilometers) when evaluated by the EPA.
While both offer highly practical real-world range, the Mercedes-AMG GT 63 gains an extra 48 miles (77 kilometers) of range on the generous European WLTP cycle thanks to its larger battery and an aggressive front-axle disconnect system that saves energy when cruising.
Expectedly, both come with high-tech cabins, but the Porsche gets more screen surface with the 14.25-inch curved OLED instrument cluster, the 12.25-inch curved OLED touchscreen, and an optional 14.9-inch display with streaming and gaming.
Photo: Porsche In the meantime, the all-new Mercedes-AMG GT 63 SUV puts all the relevant driving data in front of the driver via the 10.2-inch digital instrument cluster and most of the functions of the vehicle on the 14.0-inch center display. The AMG GT SUV also gets a passenger screen as an extra, measuring 14.0 inches.
Mercedes-AMG credited its first SUV with an ultra-low grand-tourer-like feel, topped out with a low driving position, similar to that offered by a sports coupe, while the Cayenne Turbo Electric got the typical Porsche commanding SUV view over the hood and road ahead.
And since we are comparing inches, let’s stick with that. The Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric tops out at 22 inches directly from the dealership, while Mercedes shoes its electric SUV with wheels up to 23 inches, outstyling its main rival.
It all comes down to what you get for the money The Mercedes focuses on a long, ultra-wide, slammed look that mirrors its low-slung, grand tourer seating position, while the Porsche retains more traditional, upright SUV proportions. The AMG GT is 200.2 inches (5,084 millimeters), while the Cayenne stops at 196.3 inches (4,985 millimeters). Expectedly, the Mercedes EV sports a slightly longer wheelbase compared to that of the Porsche’s EV: 119.7 inches (3,040 millimeters) versus 119.0 inches (3,023 millimeters).
Photo: Mercedes-AMG The Mercedes-AMG GT 63 SUV is equipped with the AMG Active Ride Control+, which throws out conventional mechanical anti-roll bars in favor of triple-stage adjustable air springs combined with specialized active hydraulic elements to prevent the typical squatting or nose-diving on full throttle.
Porsche fitted its Active Ride onto its SUV. The system generates massive independent vertical forces at each wheel. This means that, rather than just absorbing road imperfections, the setup makes the SUV lean into corners like a motorcycle to offset lateral forces, elevating the ride height by 2.16 inches (55 millimeters) when the doors unlock to make entry and exit easier.
The Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric starts at $163,000 in the United States, while the price jumps to $172,700 for the sleeker, sloped-roofline Coupe. Mercedes has yet to disclose the pricing of the AMG GT 63 SUV and its siblings, the GT 55 and GT 53. However, the range-topping variant is expected to hit the $200,000 mark before fees and options.

Article brought to you by Evolutionary Operating System, Inc.
For decades, the freight industry’s biggest technology investments have gone to the biggest freight companies. Enterprise carriers and mega-brokerages with dedicated engineering teams have adopted increasingly sophisticated transportation management systems and software integrations. Meanwhile, many small-to-medium-sized businesses are running TMS platforms that are sometimes a decade or more old. Even if not, they’re typically paying enterprise prices for software that wasn’t built around how a smaller operation actually runs.
This imbalance is the starting point for Evolutionary Operating System, Inc . (Evos), an autonomous AI operations company launching to the public on October 14. The reasoning, according to founder and CEO Urav Shah, runs in a fairly straight line: decades of technology investment have gone almost entirely to the enterprise end of the market, leaving small and mid-size logistics companies running on aging systems that were never built around how differently each of those businesses actually operates.
Those systems can handle the routine, predictable share of the work, but not the edge cases, such as the judgment calls that don’t fit a standard workflow. That work falls back on a person to notice, decide and process by hand. Shah argues that’s created a structural capacity problem for small and mid-size logistics companies, one that’s compounding as the industry’s most experienced operators retire and take tacit knowledge with them.
“There’s been twenty to thirty years of big tech ignoring the small and mid-market,” Shah said. “That’s created a real capacity gap. Evos is the only company that does the work instead of just showing you the work.”
What Shah describes is a platform that configures itself around a given business, learning how that company’s own team uses judgment to work through its edge cases, then handling that work on their behalf rather than simply flagging it for a person to finish.
That’s the execution layer, and it’s how Shah draws the line between Evos and the wave of AI copilots and assistants now built into most major TMS platforms. Those tools still need someone to drive them, and they’re largely unequipped to handle the edge cases that make up a vast portion of day-to-day tasks in smaller operations. Some AI agents might suggest a status update or flag an exception, but a person still has to act on it.
Because Evos was designed to be an execution layer, it can help run entire desks, such as dispatch, track-and-trace, or billing, end to end, on top of an organization’s existing systems.
The biggest challenge, according to Shah, is not just building software that can act. It’s building software that acts the way a specific company would. Every logistics operation runs a little differently, and that variation shows up constantly in the edge cases that consume an ops team’s day.
Shah gave an example of the kind of interrogation Evos runs during onboarding to capture that logic. Why did a given load go on one truck instead of another available one? Because that customer gets priority service. Why not the newer truck? Because it was already committed to a spot load with tighter lead time. Multiply that by every recurring judgment call a dispatcher makes, and the pattern of behavior is the configuration data that lets Evos’ autonomous operator match the specific execution needs of that one company rather than applying a generic workflow across every customer.
In a deliberate architectural choice, Evos runs what it calls large action models rather than large language models. The system is trained on patterns of decisions and behavior rather than on text. Every customer has its own model, trained solely on that company’s own historical data, with no shared central model pooling information across customers. Reinforcement learning happens on anonymized behavioral patterns specific to that one operation.
Shah said the approach is a direct response to a hesitation he hears constantly from smaller operators: reluctance to hand over proprietary operational knowledge to an external AI platform. Keeping each customer’s model self-contained means that tribal knowledge stays tribal. It’s neither contaminated by the way other companies behave nor at risk of any IP infringements.
Shah also points to how Evos builds those models as a further differentiator from other point-solution automations. Most of those tools run on top of frontier large language models from major AI labs, which ties their underlying costs to whatever those labs are charging at any given time. Because Evos trains and runs its own models rather than routing requests through a frontier model, Shah argues its cost structure stays fixed instead of exposed to that volatility, which he expects to matter more as frontier-model pricing eventually shifts to reflect what those labs actually spend on compute.
Tacit knowledge retention extends to how Evos is addressing the industry’s aging workforce. As ops teams around the country struggle to replace experienced talent, Evos has built a way to preserve what a retiring dispatcher or fleet manager knows before it disappears from the business entirely, and expanded the capacity of existing teams in the process. That includes things like the escalation logic, the workarounds, and the decision criteria that were never written down for a new hire to learn.
None of that works, though, if deployment takes the months typical of an enterprise software rollout. Evos says a new autonomous operator can go live in under 24 hours from first conversation, without migrating a customer’s existing data, using a library of more than 150 pre-built integrations with common freight systems.
Shah described a graduated-autonomy model for how those operators earn trust once deployed: a new operator starts by handling a portion of a workflow autonomously while routing judgment calls to a human for approval, rejection, or revision, and the system reasons from those revisions going forward. If it’s told once to avoid an older truck that needs more frequent fuel stops on a tight-deadline load, it can start weighing that same tradeoff on future loads without being told again.
As an illustration of the kind of problem Evos is building toward for smaller carriers specifically, Shah pointed to an operator currently in development that scans a carrier’s planned routes for backhaul opportunities (a truck headed from Chicago to New York with nothing booked for the return leg, for example) and surfaces a set of matching loads for a dispatcher to confirm. Today, he said, that kind of open capacity is usually found manually, often scrambled together at the last minute, if it’s found at all.
Most AI tools still need constant prompting: someone has to ask, review, and act on every answer. An Evos operator is given a function, not a prompt, so the team ends up managing outcomes instead of inputs.
One freight brokerage, MyFreightWorld, runs an Evos operator that audits every LTL carrier invoice against its TMS. In its first two months, the operator made nearly 3,500 audit decisions at 97% accuracy, and in the last five weeks alone it has closed out more than $600,000 of invoice value.
“Evos has helped us revolutionize our billing process with zero upfront investment, and also at an impressively fast speed measured in days and weeks,” said Mike Chalfant, president of MyFreightWorld. “It’s increased our accuracy and dramatically increased efficiency, which has ultimately led to a better experience for our customer base. The performance of the operator has given us confidence and excitement to continue to add to the functionality and explore new possibilities. Adding Evos to the stack has been a terrific thing for our company, and we’re excited to continue to grow our partnership.”
Those numbers point back to the same argument, according to Shah. The technology gap in freight software is largely the result of who enterprise vendors built for.
“We’re the only company that does the work instead of just showing you the work,” Shah said. While the largest carriers are already investing heavily in automation, the small and mid-size operators need a tailored solution they won’t find elsewhere.
That’s why, according to Shah, Evos’ autonomous operators are designed to help the logistics businesses most exposed to the industry’s capacity gap and the most likely to lose institutional knowledge as their veteran staff retire.

Captona LLC, a North American investment firm, has announced its latest preferred equity investment in partnership with Nexamp, a fully-integrated distributed generation and community solar company.
The investment announced October 13 support the financing of 55 MW of solar generation and 5 MWh of battery storage capacity across 10 projects in four states (Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York). The transaction marks the next phase in Captona’s continued innovation of its preferred-equity solution, highlighting the team’s ability to deploy capital with flexibility and scale.
Captona has been a market leader since rolling out its preferred equity structure in 2023. Partnering with an industry-leading solar developer in Nexamp represents a step forward in Captona’s preferred equity program and demonstrates the trust it has built with industry leaders.
“We’re proud to invest in projects delivered by a best-in-class company like Nexamp, demonstrating Captona’s ability to meet the evolving needs of our partners,” said Izzet Bensusan, CEO and founder of Captona. “As power demand continues to accelerate, we’re further scaling our investments to support our partners and the development of critical energy infrastructure.”
“Meeting rising energy demand requires us to bring new generation online quickly, and that takes strong, flexible partnerships across the industry,” said Anjali Patel, vice president of Capital Markets & Strategy at Nexamp. “This investment from Captona will help advance a diverse portfolio of solar and storage projects that can deliver meaningful benefits to individuals and communities—from greater access to local clean energy to stronger, more resilient power systems.”
Kirkland & Ellis LLP served as legal advisor to Captona, while Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP served as legal advisors to Nexamp in connection with the transaction.
Captona is a leading North America-focused energy transition investment firm with close to $3.5 billion in enterprise value, Captona owns and operates more than 50 energy generation projects, with a focus on storage, solar, microgrids, fuel cell, and renewable natural gas technologies.
Nexamp provides solar and storage solutions. The company has almost 1.5 GW of renewable energy-generating assets currently in operation and several more gigawatts under construction or in development.
—This content was contributed by the communications team for Captona .

Jay Leno Gets Up Close and Personal With Hennessey Blackbird: Zero Screens and No Electrification
14 photos
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube
Meet the 2029 Hennessey Blackbird before you are actually supposed to meet it. The Blackbird is the upcoming, ultra-exclusive, all-analog hypercar, designed as an act of rebellion against modern electrified vehicles with cabins covered in screens. This is the car that Jay Leno now gets up close and personal with long before deliveries even start.
Jay Leno and John Hennessey have a history together. They first met back in 1993. At the time, John was a hot rodder who turned Dodge Vipers into venomous machines. Since then, he has built three insane hypercars. First came the Hennessey Venom GT with 1,244 horsepower (1,261 metric horsepower). A decade later, he came up with the Venom F5 in standard form, boasting 1,817 horsepower (1,842 metric horsepower).
In January 2026, the Venom F5 Evolution broke cover with a mind-blowing 2,031 horsepower (2,059 metric horsepower). Now, he has come up with the Blackbird, which is unlike any car he has built before. It comes with the most powerful naturally aspirated V8 ever put in a road-going production car.
But with no supercharger, turbocharger, or electrification, the Hennessey Blackbir d is more about the driver than about speed and horsepower. It is unlike anything John Hennessey has ever built and something that nobody would expect from him.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Nathan Malinick , head of design at Hennessey, brought an SR-71 Blackbird prototype to Jay Leno’s Garage to tell the story that has just begun. The 2029 Hennessey Blackbird was officially unveiled during the Monterey Car Week in August 2026 under the codename "Project Overlord."
The hypercar trades straight-line performance for absolute driver engagement, drawing inspiration from the legendary Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird reconnaissance aircraft. There is a crease stretching along the side pod, imitating the plane’s chine line.
The diamond-shaped headlights are actually inspired by the inlet spikes on the front of the SR-71 Blackbird's engines, which moved back and forth to control airflow at supersonic speeds, while the rear lights mimic the glowing afterburners of the jet. The quad-exhaust array at the rear of the Hennessey Blackbird is directly inspired by the four rocket nozzles on Chuck Yeager's Bell X-1.
The Blackbird rides on lightweight forged wheels, measuring 20 inches up front and 21 inches out back, wrapped in off-the-shelf Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires with nothing custom about them. Brembo carbon ceramic brakes provide the stopping power.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Developed in partnership with Ilmor Engineering, the engine that powers it is somewhat of a masterpiece: a high-revving, mid-mounted 6.2-liter V8 with naturally aspirated firepower, with a target output between 800 and 850 horsepower, redlining at an incredible 9,000 rpm.
A six-speed gated manual transmission sends power to the ground through the rear wheels. Who would have thought there would still be manual cars in 2029? The model is expected to hit 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill in 2.5 seconds and max out at 220 mph (354 kph).
Sure, there are hypercars out there that come with more than 850 horsepower, but not many of them sport such a lightweight architecture. The Blackbird is built completely from a carbon fiber monocoque tub and carbon body panels. That is why it tips the scales at under 3,000 pounds (1,361 kilograms).
The Hennessey-badged model features aerospace-inspired active vertical stabilizers that automatically deploy at 71 mph (114 kph) at an angle of 71 degrees. “That is the Blackbird flying,” Nathan Malinick explains.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube The doors of the prototype that was parked in Jay Leno’s Garage don’t open. But when they do, they will be dihedral synchro-helix or butterfly-style doors, providing access to a cabin that completely rejects digital trends. The dashboard is entirely screenless in an era in which automakers are struggling to offer the largest screen surface on board their vehicles. Instead, it features five traditional analog dials and a large central tachometer.
Because the car has a solid rear bulkhead and an engine cover that blocks the view out the back window, an actual rearview mirror would be useless. However, to get around this while staying legal for road use, Hennessey uses a digital rearview mirror. There is a camera on the back, streaming a live, high-definition video onto a hidden display built inside the glass of the rearview mirror.
An exposed manual shift linkage, physical switches, and a completely buttonless steering wheel are also on the menu, along with a classic ignition key and a roof-mounted start button. The cabin also hosts a mechanical whiskey compass, the type used in early aviation and marine navigation for those moments when the driver has no Google Maps or Waze available.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube It is called a "whiskey" compass because the glass bowl housing the magnetic card is filled with a clear fluid, an alcohol-water mix like whiskey or pure ethanol to dampen vibrations and stop the compass needle from swinging wildly.
Instead of a digital clock, the Hennessey Blackbird will come with a removable dash-top timepiece with a high-end luxury mechanical design, styled after the aircraft chronometers from the mid-20th century, which pilots used to time flight legs. The clock features a quick-release mechanism, so that the driver can unlock it from the dashboard dock and wear it as a wristwatch or place it into a desk stand when they are done driving.
The Blackbird has also been designed with practicality in mind. The front trunk is specifically sized to fit two airline-approved carry-on flight cases, because the car was designed with the wives in mind, says Nathan. There is also an integrated luggage space behind the front seats, alongside unique exterior saddlebag compartments built into the lifting rear quarter panels. It sounds like it’s got the most luggage space of all hypercars.
Hennessey will only build 71 units, each starting at an eye-watering $2.5 million . Customer deliveries are scheduled to kick off in 2029.

There are plenty of ways to make an electric motorcycle stand out, but putting a giant hole through the middle of it is certainly one of the more effective options.
German electric motorcycle startup NOVUS has announced a new funding round worth “double-digit millions of dollars,” money that will help fund the company’s expansion into the US in 2027 as well as further European growth. The company says its NOVUS One is already in series production, with European deliveries beginning earlier this year.
It’s an important update from a company we first covered so long ago that mass mask-wearing was still seen as a foreign concept.
The NOVUS One is one of the more unusual-looking electric motorcycles on the road, largely thanks to its large carbon fiber monocoque frame. The self-supporting structure wraps around a cavernous opening where you’d normally expect to find much of a motorcycle’s bodywork.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
That striking design comes from NOVUS founder René Renger, a former Volkswagen lead designer who worked on vehicles including the Golf and ID. Buzz. NOVUS says design, engineering, and final assembly are all performed in Germany, with most components sourced from Europe.
Despite the minimalist appearance, there’s some serious performance hiding in that skinny package.
The NOVUS One weighs just 121 kg (267 lb), considerably lighter than many conventional motorcycles. Its hub-mounted drivetrain produces up to 25 kW (33 hp) of peak power and a claimed 430 Nm of torque in its highest-performance mode.
That’s enough for 0-50 km/h (31 mph) acceleration in under two seconds and a top speed of 130 km/h (81 mph).
The 6.2 kWh battery is rated for up to 150 km (93 miles) of range at lower city speeds, while a 0-80% charge takes a claimed 90 minutes. There are three riding modes, smartphone integration, keyless operation, and over-the-air updates.
Interestingly, NOVUS can also configure the same hardware through software for two different vehicle classes.
The full-power L3e version reaches 130 km/h, while an L1e version is limited to 45 km/h (28 mph), effectively turning the same exotic-looking machine into a scooter-class vehicle. Licensing requirements vary by market.
NOVUS calls the One a “Lightbike,” positioning it somewhere between a scooter and a motorcycle.
The company’s pitch is that the low weight, lack of clutch or gears, and simple electric drivetrain can make two-wheeled transportation approachable even for people who don’t consider themselves motorcyclists.
There is one rather large catch: price.
The NOVUS One Founders Edition starts at €21,300 before tax. That’s a lot of money for an urban electric motorcycle, even one that looks like someone accidentally deleted the middle third of the bike in Photoshop, and a bares an uncomfortably close passing resemblance to the ill-fated Metacycle .
NOVUS says a second, higher-volume model called the NOVUS Two is already in development, with production planned for late 2027 at a “significantly lower” entry price.
And that may ultimately be the more important machine. Because the NOVUS One certainly proves that an electric motorcycle can turn heads. Now NOVUS has to prove it can turn that attention into riders.

Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross with the 37 kWh battery, starting at about $31,000 (€27,995).
Volkswagen ID. Cross with 37 kWh battery goes on sale
The ID. Cross is a “true Volkswagen,” the brand’s CEO Thomas Schäfer said last month after the electric SUV entered production at its Pamplona, Spain, plant.
As the electric equivalent of its best-selling T-Cross, Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above, all affordable.” It follows the ID. Polo as the first electric SUV from its new entry-level EV lineup.
As promised, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend this week, starting at €27,995 in Germany, including VAT, or about $31,500.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The new variant uses a 37 kWh battery and a 114 hp (85 kW) electric motor, providing a WLTP range of up to 201 miles (324 km).
Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery in July, with a WLTP range of up to 265 miles (427 km).
Volkswagen ID. Cross with the 37 kWh battery goes on sale in Germany (Source: Volkswagen Germany)
It’s based on the same MEB+ platform as the ID. Polo. The VW ID. Cross is now available with two battery packs: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack, and three variants:
VW ID. Cross Trend: standard with 85 kW (114 hp) and 37‑kWh battery
VW ID. Cross Life and ID. Cross Style: standard with 99 kW (132 hp) and 37‑kWh battery
VW ID. Cross Life and ID. Cross Style: optional with 155 kW (207 hp) and 52‑kWh battery
With DC fast charging up to 90 kW, the smaller 37 kWh battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 23 minutes. The 52 kWh battery takes around 24 minutes to charge from 10% to 80% with DC fast charging up to 105 kW.
Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s new interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ “Digital Cockpit Pro” instrument display and a 12.9″ center infotainment screen.
Volkswagen ID. Cross concept interior (Source: Volkswagen)
Like the ID. Polo and ID. Tiguan, the electric SUV features a new Retro Display mode that turns the instrument panel into a throwback theme reminiscent of the first-gen Golf 1.
The electric version is 4,161 mm long, 1,794 mm wide, and 1,588 mm high, with a 2,601 mm wheelbase, or about the size of the gas-powered Volkswagen T-Cross.
Starting at €27,995 ($31,500), the ID. Cross sits between the T-Cross (€25,280) and Tiguan (€39,385) in price.
Volkswagen has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US, but it will launch the ID. Tiguan in early 2027 as the ID.4’s replacement.

A superconducting neural network chip that borrows tricks from quantum computers has successfully passed a battery of tests that involved processing data from a fusion reactor. The Genesis Mission project paves the way to the development of a bigger chip for more fusion testing next year, and showcases the potential for a new type of silicon that could leapfrog current energy and performance limits of GPUs in supercomputers.
Great Sky is a Boulder, Colorodo chip startup that was spun out of the National Institute of Standards and Technology by CEO Jeff Shainline and his co-founders in 2024 following nearly a decade of development at NIST. The company, which came out of stealth in March, is developing a chip that utilizes technologies often found in quantum computers, such as superconducting compute and optical connectivity, to implement an analog neural network in hardware, rather than just emulating one digitally.
Great Sky’s neuromorphic chip (Image courtesy Great Sky)
Great Sky says its approach, which it dubs superconducting optoelectronic network (SOEN), can process data at significantly higher rates than traditional chips, such as GPUs, given the same energy. The key to the high performance of Great Sky’s SOEN approach is the combination of superconducting Josephson junction circuits, which offer the highest speed-to-energy ratio of any known circuit element, along with integrated photonic waveguides for long-range, single-photon optical communication, the company says.
“We use many of the same devices as quantum technologies–superconducting circuits, single-photon detectors–but we use them for classical, analog computation in a parallel, distributed architecture, which is ideal for AI,” CEO Shainline said in a blog post earlier this year.
“By constructing new hardware that enables more sophisticated architectures and algorithms while performing operations near the physical limits of speed and energy efficiency, we can transition to a completely different roadmap for scaling that doesn’t require hundreds of billions in capex and gigawatt data centers,” he added.
Those claims were tested in a series of Genesis Mission-related challenges put together by Great Sky, Brookhaven National Lab , Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory , and the DIII-D National Fusion Facility operated by General Atomics in San Diego, California. Brookhaven led the development of a specialized chip based on Great Sky’s technology that was used to manage the tokamak at the heart of the DIII-D fusion reactor, the largest operating tokamak in North America.
Brookhaven said the new chip had “no problem” processing data from the tokamak at rates up to one million data samples per second.
Great Sky CEO and Co-founder Jeffrey Shainline
“This chip took data straight from a tokamak at millions of samples every second and kept up,” said Steven Cowley, laboratory director of PPP, which was involved in the testing. “That’s a real step toward practical fusion power, and I can’t wait to see where we take it next.”
The neuromorphic chip also passed with flying colors a simulated test from a tokamak simulator developed by the Google DeepMind fusion team, dubbed TORAX, that checks how well a system can respond to rapidly changing plasma behavior in a fusion reaction.
Great Sky, which has completed four chip tapeouts for under $4 million, is planning to build another chip with neural network that’s 10x bigger. The goal is to have the chip completed by the end of the year and ready for testing at Brookhaven Lab in early 2027, followed by another onsite deployment at the DIII-D tokamak later in the year.
“It’s incredible to see the team processing data from our tokamak,” said Richard Buttery, the director of DIII-D. “The folks here at DIII-D are very excited to see how this chip can impact diagnostics and control for the fusion industry.”
Managing fusion reactors is one potential use case of Great Sky’s superconducting neural network chip, but there are others. Ultimately, the goal of Great Sky–which was awarded a phase one contract with the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission project–is to build supercomputers with more neurons and synapses than the human brain, operating a million times faster.
“This is our largest chip to date, and it’s great to see it processing high-speed data directly measured from a tokamak,” stated Shainline. “But this is just the beginning. This approach to AI hardware has so much to offer with regard to fusion, as well as other applications at the forefront of technology. Control and error correction of quantum systems, advanced cybersecurity, video intelligence with continual learning–these are all incredible opportunities as we scale up our systems.”
Generating tokens for AI is another use case. According to Great Sky, its neuromorphic chip could potentially generate 1 million output tokens for one penny, which is 300x less expensive than the best AI hardware can do today, or $3 per 1m tokens.

Arizona’s first three NEVI-funded DC fast-charging stations are finally online, giving EV drivers more places to plug in along I-10, I-19, and I-8.
Getting here took years of planning and procurement, with a Trump administration funding freeze disrupting the state’s broader rollout along the way.
The new Arizona NEVI fast chargers are in Tucson, Green Valley, and Wellton:
Tucson: Tesla Supercharger, 325 kW, Rudy’s Country Store and Bar-B-Q, 2130 E. Ajo Way, near I-10 and Kino Parkway
Green Valley: Francis, 400 kW, Verde Valley Center, 119 E. Duval Mine Road, off I-19
Wellton: Tesla Supercharger, 325 kW, Chevron, 28864 Commerce Way, near I-8 and Avenue 29 E
They’re the first operating sites in Arizona’s plan to use some of the $76.5 million in federal funding to build as many as 79 stations statewide.

Why did Arizona’s first NEVI stations take so long?
The National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program was created by the Biden administration’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law in 2021. But Arizona didn’t begin taking bids for its first round of DC fast-charging stations until January 2024, after developing its deployment plan and working through federal requirements. The first awards followed in August 2024.
Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT) initially said construction would take about a year after final contracts were signed, with some locations expected to open by late 2025. Construction ultimately began in early 2026.
Then came the sabotage. In February 2025, the Trump administration suspended states’ approved NEVI plans and blocked new funding commitments while it rewrote the program’s guidance. Reimbursements under existing project agreements were allowed to continue.
That had a direct consequence in Arizona: Court records show the state canceled a solicitation for 35 prospective charging locations after losing access to roughly $48.1 million in funding that hadn’t yet been committed to projects.
Arizona joined the states challenging the freeze. A federal judge granted preliminary relief in June 2025 and ruled in January 2026 that the funding had been unlawfully withheld. So the timeline includes both Arizona’s lengthy initial procurement and a federal interruption that set back its next round of stations. The records don’t establish how much the freeze delayed each of the three sites now open.
What’s next?
Next up are Seligman and Holbrook along I-40, where two more stations are expected to open before the end of 2026.
ADOT now says most stations will offer both NACS and CCS plugs, with at least four 150-kilowatt DC fast chargers at most locations, as required by NEVI. Its opening announcement doesn’t provide a connector-by-connector breakdown for the three operating sites.
ADOT is also seeking bids for 49 locations, backed by an estimated $49 million in federal funding. That round includes 31 new locations and 18 previously unawarded sites. Proposals are due January 15, 2027; construction is expected to start in 2028 and take about a year.

NTPC Limited, India’s largest electric utility, has signed a power purchase agreement with 247 Solar and will deploy that company’s Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) technology as part of its energy strategy.
The companies on October 15 said it will mark the first commercial project for 247 Solar and its solar thermal tech. The Virginia-based company has said the deal is a milestone as 247 Solar improves on the first generation of its technology, which is designed to overcome the intermittency of conventional solar power.
NTPC said it will test whether 247 Solar’s system can help the utility reduce its reliance on coal-fired power generation as India expands its use of renewable energy. Officials said the project, if successful, would likely enable an expansion of 247 Solar’s technology across India.
Advanced CSP
“This new version of solar thermal solves the problem of intermittent solar and wind power, and avoids spending more on outdated, costly, and dirty coal plants,” said Bruce Anderson, founder and CEO of 247Solar. “India’s rapid growth plainly requires more clean, reliable and affordable energy. Our system can help meet that demand. I’m thrilled that after several years of deep due diligence, NTPC is working with us to bring this promising technology into wider use.”
247Solar has said its technology removes the drawbacks of previous CSP technology. The system still captures the sun’s heat with mirrors focused on towers, but the new version is simplified, modular, and scalable. It simultaneously provides heat up to 1,000C (more than 1,800F) for industrial processes, according to the company.
Artist’s conception of a 247Solar Plant like the one NTPC, India’s largest electric utility, plans to deploy at Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan, India. Mirrors concentrate sunlight on a tower, and ceramic pellets store the heat for up to 20 hours to run turbines without combustion. Source: 247 Solar
The system, according to 247 Solar, “stores heat for up to 20 hours in ceramic pellets, using hot air to generate electricity around the clock with unique turbines that operate without combustion under normal conditions. If the stored heat runs low overnight or during extended cloudy weather, the same turbines can also run on liquid or gaseous fuels, including natural gas, green hydrogen, or diesel, so the plant can keep producing power without interruption.”
247 Solar said the new technology has several benefits compared with traditional CSP:
Lower cost.
Speed to power.
Simplicity of design and operation.
High reliability.
Grid independence.
Cost-effective baseload power.
The company said the NTPC project is a ~1MW hybrid, integrating one 400-kW modular 247Solar Plant with several hundred kilowatts of photovoltaic solar. It is being installed at Rajasthan’s Bhadla Solar Park, which is among the world’s largest solar energy hubs, in an arid region in northwestern India. The project is backed by the Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation Limited, which has approved preliminary studies, site surveys, and structural tests. NTPC and 247Solar said the companies selected the location for its abundant sunshine, and for its easy interconnection for offtake of its energy output.
The groups said the demonstration “marks an early step toward round-the-clock clean power for industry and residents in India,” and added that “success will position Rajasthan as a proving ground for the technology and give NTPC a new tool as it works to meet the country’s growing power demand while reducing reliance on coal, cutting costs and carbon emissions simultaneously.”
— Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

A New Mexico jury has awarded $47 million to a pick up truck driver and his mother in a lawsuit against Pilot Thomas Logistics LLC and Maxum Petroleum Operating Company stemming from a 2022 head-on collision involving a commercial tanker truck.
The verdict followed a jury trial in the First Judicial District Court in Tierra Amarilla, New Mexico, involving Austin Drewry Jackson, who was 21 at the time of the crash, and his mother, Crystal Gayle Drewry.
The $47 million verdict is among the largest reported trucking accident awards in New Mexico in recent years.
The New Mexico verdict follows a separate $104 million jury award in July against Mesilla Valley Transportation in a fatal truck crash lawsuit in Texas.
The award also comes amid growing concerns about so-called nuclear verdicts — jury awards exceeding $10 million — and their impact on trucking companies’ insurance costs and financial stability.
According to an Oct. 13 blog post from the plaintiffs’ attorneys at Tawney, Acosta & Chaparro P.C., the November 2022 crash occurred on a two-lane highway near Carlsbad, New Mexico.
The law firm alleged that the commercial tanker truck driver was traveling too fast for weather conditions and failed to see or react to Drewry’s approaching vehicle before the head-on collision.
A 2025 American Transportation Research Institute study found that allegations of speeding and other pre-crash negligence can significantly increase jury awards against trucking companies.
Drewry suffered severe traumatic brain injuries, along with extensive damage to his spine, bones and internal organs, according to the firm.
Drewry, a Louisiana native who joined the Louisiana National Guard at age 18 and served on two deployments, was working on an oil rig in New Mexico when the collision occurred. He had planned to return home for Thanksgiving.
“The defense’s first pretrial offer of $100,000 did not come close to acknowledging the harm Austin suffered or the care he will need,” James Tawney, a partner at Tawney, Acosta & Chaparro, said in a statement.
Court records reviewed by FreightWaves confirm that the lawsuit, Austin Drewry Jackson et al. v. Pilot Thomas Logistics LLC et al. , was filed April 26, 2024, under Case No. D-117-CV-2024-00161.
The case was heard before District Judge Francis J. Mathew. Jury selection began Oct. 5, and the court docket lists a special verdict form filed Oct. 13.
The court also granted a motion Oct. 7 dismissing claims against truck driver Marcos Alejandro Romero in his individual capacity, with prejudice. The case proceeded against the corporate defendants.
The docket shows that the defendants filed motions Oct. 9 challenging the plaintiffs’ claims involving punitive damages, direct negligence, proximate cause and loss of consortium.
The publicly available docket does not specify how the $47 million verdict was allocated among damages categories or whether punitive damages were included.
As of Oct. 19, the docket did not list a separately entered final judgment or notice of appeal.
Why it matters: The New Mexico verdict highlights the potentially enormous financial exposure facing trucking companies in injury lawsuits.

Junkyard Dog 1979 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am Has the Great W72 Powertrain, It Will Make Grown Men Cry
36 photos
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society
Tucked between a mundane Chevrolet Impala and a weathered Buick Park Avenue in a sun-baked salvage yard, a stripped 1979 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am rests precariously on stacked steel wheel rims. Documented by Benny Sanchez, the host of the Classic Ride Society YouTube channel, and avid derelict Detroit iron hunter, this battered coupe hides a remarkable secret beneath its peeling paint: a factory 400-cubic-inch, paired with a 4-speed manual drivetrain.
This junkyard inmate’s history can be traced back almost sixty years ago, with the debut of the Pontiac Firebird moniker. The Pontiac pony car was deliberately launched on 23 February 1967 as a corporate counterpart to Chevrolet's Camaro – and it was that precise reason that delayed the Firebird by five months.
GM wanted something to take on the Mustangs, and the Chevy Camaro was given the right of way, putting the Poncho in a cone shadow. Although it was one of the two true pony cars that soldiered on through the seventies (while the Mustang was a Pinto in disguise), the Firebird didn’t have the same public appeal as the Chevy.
Mind you, it wasn’t a poor-selling machine at all; it just wasn’t as good as the Camaro. Built across four generations over 36 model years, total Firebird production reached 2,614,563 units, comprising 277,380 first-generation cars from 1967 to 1969, 1,179,407 second-gens over 12 model years (1970 to 1981), 840,597vehicles between 1982 and 1992, and a final 317,179 production total for the fourth and final iteration (1993 to 2002).
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society In March 1969, two full years after the Firebird debuted, Pontiac introduced the Trans Am performance package, paying a $5 royalty per vehicle to the Sports Car Club of America for using its series name. Built across 34 model years from 1969 to 2002, Trans Am volumes totaled 927,210 units, consisting of 697 first-generation cars in 1969, 459,213 second-generation models, 332,480 third-generation cars, and 134,820 fourth-generation models produced through August 2002.
The 1979 model year marked the 10-year anniversary of the Trans Am moniker and brought freshly restyled urethane front fascias with quad rectangular headlamps alongside full-width slotted taillights. Despite tightening emissions standards and rising fuel costs, 1979 set an all-time Firebird production record of 211,453 cars, divided by model into 38,642 base Firebirds, 30,853 luxury Esprits including 4,248 Redbird editions, 24,850 twin-scoop Formulas, and a record 117,108 Trans Am coupes.
Coincidence or not, the Camaro also sold its all-time best volumes (282,582 ponies). It was also the year of the fox-body Mustang, which absolutely crashed the Chevy-Poncho party and completely stole the show with 369,936 debuting third-gen cars.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society For 1979, the cheapest Trans Am carried a base price of $6,299 and came standard with the RPO L80 403-cubic-inch (advertised in the traditional Pontiac European spelling “6.6-litre”) Oldsmobile four-barrel V8 paired with the RPO MX1 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic 350 automatic transmission.
Breathing through a reverse-mounted shaker hood scoop, that standard Olds engine was good for 185 horsepower at 3,600 rpm and 315 lb-ft-ft of torque at 2,000 rpm, and it came exclusively with an automatic transmission.
Two optional V8s and an extra-cost manual gearbox completed the 1979 Trans Am lineup. Buyers prioritizing fuel economy could specify the RPO L37 301-cuber, Pontiac’s 4.9-liter, four-barrel V8, rated at 150 horsepower at 4,000 rpm and 240 lb-ft at 2,000 rpm, which provided a $150 credit and could be mated to either the standard 3-speed automatic transmission or the no-cost optional RPO M21 close-ratio 4-speed manual transmission.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society Enthusiasts demanding maximum performance ordered the RPO W72 motor, Pontiac’s true apex predator: 400-cubic-inch (marked with “T/A 6.6” on the hood scoop) Pontiac single-quad V8. PMD actually stockpiled whatever 400 blocks it could at the end of 1978 for one final glorious anniversary run.
Rated at 220 horsepower at 4,000 rpm and 320 lb-ft of torque at 2,800 rpm, the $90 optional 400-incher required the no-cost Borg-Warner Super T-10 4-speed manual transmission and the mandatory $434 WS6 Special Performance Package, adding $524 to a standard Trans Am sticker.
Breaking down the 117,108 Trans Ams built for 1979 reveals how buyers configured their cars across four sub-models and two transmissions. Overall, 105,449 customers chose the 3-speed automatic transmission, while only 11,659 selected the 4-speed manual gearbox.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society Body-wise, Pontiac produced 59,578 standard hardtop coupes, 38,476 T-Tops with the $655 CC1 removable glass panels, 11,554 Y84 Black Special Edition coupes ($1,329 extra), and 7,500 Y89 TATAs (Tenth Anniversary Trans Am) coupes, priced at an eyewatering $10,619.
Separating those 117,108 Trans Ams by engine and transmission highlights the scarcity of manual-shift cars. The standard 403 V8 and automatic transmission powered 94,773 examples, comprising 48,488 hardtop coupes, 30,728 T-Top coupes, 9,874 Black Special Editions, and 5,683 10th Anniversary editions.
The 301 V8 accounted for 14,009 cars, split into 7,015 automatic and 1,590 manual hardtops, 3,301 automatic and 1,530 manual T-Tops, and 360 automatic and 213 manual Special Editions.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society That leaves just 8,326 Trans Ams, alongside 346 Formulas, equipped with the W72 400-cubic-inch Pontiac V8 and 4-speed manual transmission in 1979. Across the four Trans Am sub-models, Pontiac built 2,485 hardtop coupes, 1,107 Y84 Black Special Editions, 1,817 Y89 10th Anniversary models, and 2,917 T-Tops. This junkyard find is one of those 2,917 T-Top 400 4-speeds (that’s 2.49 percent of the grand total of Trans Ams).
Built on the fourth week of October 1978, and sprayed in Heritage Brown Metallic paint with the $150 Camel cloth interior, this sore sight for nostalgic eyes was quite the brawler back in its heyday. Truth be told, that 220-hp rating was a bit downplayed – real-world testing placed it closer to 260 net, which was about the best thing money could buy in 1979.
Just for reference, America’s Sportscar, the Corvette, offered a 225-horse 350-cube small-block V8 as the top dog. The Trans Am, naturally, couldn’t take the spotlight away from GM’s favorite child – in brochures, at least – but it sure had it its way on the street. Well, that’s all long gone now, with this boneyard dog having made peace with the thought that the only way out of there is though the smelting furnace.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Ride Society Decades of neglect in the elements have taken a heavy toll on the Heritage Brown Metallic bodywork. With the shaker hood, carburetor, valve covers, and exhaust long gone, rainwater has pooled inside the venerable 400 V8 block. Previous scavengers have already stripped the slotted rear taillights, cracked the rear decklid spoiler, and removed the wheels.
Despite the missing 15x8-inch aluminum Snowflake wheels, which the car hunter now kicks himself for passing up years ago when they were around $300, the undercarriage retains unmistakable WS6 Special Performance Package hardware. Rusted rotors and calipers on all four corners confirm the factory J65 4-wheel power disc brakes, complemented by a thick front sway bar and front wheel spoilers he plans to salvage for his own 1977 Firebird Formula, and vintage Rocket traction bars.
Both doors remain jammed shut, and even a pair of bolt cutters borrowed from a nearby pickup bed fails to pry the driver latch open. Peering through the shattered window glass and open T-Top roof reveals a loose tilt steering column, sun-baked Camel Tan hobnail cloth seats draped in tattered sheepskin covers, an empty 1987 Roger Troutman cassette case, and the chrome Hurst shifter handle of that 4-speed manual transmission.
Speaking of which, the original Borg-Warner Super T-10 cogbox and its three linkage rods remain bolted ahead of the 3.23:1 Safe-T-Track limited-slip rear axle. Although severe rust and missing body panels have pushed this rare 1979 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am beyond any hope, its powertrain components still await rescue before the crusher claims another legend.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers discovered nearly $30.4 million in suspected methamphetamine inside a commercial salt shipment in Texas. The October 12 seizure occurred at Laredo’s World Trade Bridge along the U.S.-Mexico border. Officers recovered 3,395.91 pounds of suspected methamphetamine from a 2020 International LT625 tractor-trailer. Authorities subsequently released the driver and equipment while federal investigators continued examining the case.
Officers discovered 76 bags containing suspected methamphetamine inside a trailer manifested as salt. The agency referred the investigation to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). Officials have not publicly established whether the driver or trucking company knew about the concealed drugs.
Commercial shipment leads to multimillion-dollar seizure
A CBP officer selected the commercial vehicle for additional examination during the crossing. Officers conducted a secondary inspection using nonintrusive imaging technology before uncovering the concealed narcotics.
An HSI officer examines bags associated with the methamphetamine seizure at Laredo’s World Trade Bridge. (Photos courtesy of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)
Laredo is the nation’s busiest commercial land port, handling 2.95 million inbound truck crossings from Mexico in 2025, according to federal transportation data . In September, federal investigators uncovered more than 2,000 pounds of methamphetamine concealed inside a commercial cabbage shipment in South Texas.
Driver and tractor-trailer released
FreightWaves asked why authorities released the driver and equipment. Questions also included the carrier’s identity and country of registration, importer of record and shipment destination. CBP and HSI declined to provide those details, citing the ongoing investigation.
In a statement to FreightWaves, HSI outlined its ongoing investigation. “HSI continues to investigate the matter and pursue all available leads to identify those responsible for bringing this significant quantity of methamphetamine into the United States and prevent it from reaching communities across South Texas,” the agency stated. FreightWaves will update this article as new information becomes available.
Why it matters
Commercial freight shipments can conceal substantial quantities of narcotics, placing trucking companies and drivers within federal investigations. The driver’s reported release makes the circumstances surrounding this particular shipment especially relevant to transportation professionals.

Ford Recalls Certain F-150 Trucks Over Front Seats That May Not Be Bolted Down Properly
64 photos
Photo: Ford
Somewhere in a Ford plant, a team leader typed 'repair complete' into a tracking system even if the seat was still missing a bolt. That error now costs an estimated 2,276 trucks a trip back to the dealer. FoMoCo is recalling 2025 to 2027 model year F-150 pickups because the front seats may not be properly secured to the body, increasing the risk of injury.
26V655 is the NHTSA's number for this recall, which can trace its roots back to June 2026. That's when a dealer technician found a 2026 model year F-150 with a missing driver's seat bolt and a front passenger bolt that was not fully seated. The service technician, therefore, asked the obvious question in their head.
Eventually, the technician in question escalated the issue to the Dearborn-based automaker's safety boffins. How does a truck leave the factory missing such an important bolt? Production records indicate that the primary operator at the seat workstation could not secure the seat within the workstation's cycle time. The line stopped, then an error-proofing hold released the subject trucks to the assigned repair team leader.
The TL's task was to finish the seat and log it as intended. While they may have logged it, missing or loose bolts are the reasons why this recall happened in the first place. 16 days after the dealer report landed, the Critical Concern Review Group picked up the file to investigate the matter.
Per the recall documentation filed with the federal watchdog, the bolt is cataloged with four color-matching covers for it: Black, Java, Smoked Truffle, and Navy Pier. Somebody appears to have specced trim colors for hardware that wasn't always in the seat. Through August 2026, the Ford Motor Company chases every unit the same operator had flagged for seat bolt repairs.
Photo: Ford After pulling bolt installation data from the electric tool itself, FoMoCo had all the information required to push things forward. The second-largest automaker among Detroit's Big Three is aware of 16 field reports and 56 warranty reports that are either related or potentially related to this error, totaling 62 unique VINs.
The recall population spans F-150 pickups assembled between August 25, 2025, and September 23, 2026. In the US market, an estimated 2,276 examples have to be checked. Obviously enough, customers may hear abnormal rattling noises coming from affected seats. The worst-case scenario is a seat that moves way too much for comfort.
As you might have already guessed, a loose seat connection drags restraint performance down with it when things go south. Dealers are required to verify if the bolts are present and torqued to the correct specification. If necessary, subject bolts will be replaced or retorqued as needed. Notification letters will be mailed between October 26 and October 30.
Affected VINs became searchable on the NHTSA's portal on October 9, 2026. That being said, the Ford Motor Company has made a few changes to its best-selling model in the United States of America for 2027. The biggest one is the discontinuation of the 2.7-liter EcoBoost V6.
The 2027 model year sees it replaced by a detuned version of the 3.0-liter EcoBoost V6 we normally associate with the Bronco Raptor and Ranger Raptor. In the F-150, the newcomer generates a very respectable 325 horsepower and 400 pound-feet (542 Newton-meters) of twist. By comparison, the Coyote makes 400 hp and 410 (556 lb-ft) at full chatter.

Volvo Trucks North America launched the Silver Service Contract on Monday at the American Trucking Associations ’ Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, North Carolina. The plan adds repair coverage for the engine, aftertreatment system, transmission, and clutch to the connected preventive maintenance in Volvo’s Blue Service Contract.
Truck repair and maintenance costs rose 8.6% in 2025, according to the American Transportation Research Institute’s 2026 Analysis of the Operational Costs of Trucking . The category reached 21.5 cents per mile , up from 19.8 cents in 2024. Peter Voorhoeve, president of Volvo Trucks North America, called maintenance and powertrain repairs the least predictable costs a fleet carries and said Silver puts them inside a single monthly payment.
Silver is sold through Volvo’s network of nearly 400 authorized dealers in the United States and Canada and is available for the all-new VNL and all-new VNR.
What Silver adds to Blue
Blue covers preventive maintenance. It uses connected-vehicle data and artificial intelligence to set each truck’s service schedule from its powertrain operating conditions. Those conditions include fuel consumption, transport cycle, gross combination weight, topography, and idle time, according to Volvo’s sales sheet for Silver.
Silver keeps those Blue benefits. Its powertrain coverage also extends to other select driveline components and includes the wearable clutch lining kit. When a truck comes in for an unplanned repair, any preventive maintenance that is due can be done on the same visit. Scheduled work includes valve adjustments, diesel particulate filter cleaning, diesel exhaust fluid tank flushes, and transmission and rear axle oil changes. The list varies by contract mileage.
Volvo’s third contract level, Gold, is a full-service plan sold with the VNR Electric .
Price and terms not disclosed
Volvo did not disclose what Silver costs, how long contracts run, or whether mileage caps apply. The release also does not say how Silver coverage works alongside Volvo’s standard truck warranty. Optional add-ons, including annual Department of Transportation inspections, truck washes, on-site maintenance, and pickup and delivery, vary by location.
One payment and a dealer fleet manager
Customers financing a truck through Volvo Financial Services can bundle Silver into the truck payment and spread its cost over the financing period interest-free.
Each customer works with a Volvo Fleet Manager at a certified dealer. The fleet manager plans maintenance from data the trucks send and handles service campaigns, recalls, and over-the-air software updates. More than 80% of connected Volvo trucks were running the latest software as of June .
If a truck breaks down away from its home dealer, the fleet manager coordinates with the servicing dealer through Volvo Action Service, the company’s 24/7 roadside assistance and service coordination network.
“The Volvo Fleet Manager becomes part of the customer’s team,” Voorhoeve said. “They know the fleet, they know what preventive service is due, and they handle it.”
Why it matters: Silver shifts the cost of a major powertrain failure from the fleet to Volvo for a monthly payment, bundled with financing and a dealer fleet manager. With repair and maintenance costs up 8.6% in 2025, pricing will decide whether that trade makes sense.
